entities.name: Huguo Chan Buddhist Temple of the Linji School
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Huguo Chan Buddhist Temple of the Linji School (护国禅寺, Huguo Chansi), associated with the Linji (Rinzai in Japanese) school of Chan Buddhism — the most influential school of Chinese Buddhist practice that transmitted to Japan as Rinzai Zen and to Korea as Imje Seon — represents a significant institution within one of Buddhism's most historically consequential contemplative lineages, whose emphasis on sudden enlightenment through koan (gong'an) practice, shouting, and unconventional methods profoundly shaped East Asian Buddhist culture, philosophy, and art.

The Linji school was founded by the 9th-century Tang Dynasty monk Linji Yixuan (d. 866 CE), whose teaching methods — including the famous shout (喝 hè, 'Katsu!' in Japanese) and physical blows as means to jolt students toward enlightenment — were recorded in the Linji lu (Record of Linji), one of the most important texts in Chan Buddhism. The Linji/Rinzai tradition's emphasis on koan practice (systematized in the 11th-12th centuries through collections like the Blue Cliff Record and the Gateless Gate) created one of Buddhist history's most distinctive pedagogical systems.

The Linji tradition's transmission to Japan through Eisai (1141-1215) and subsequently to the Korean peninsula created the dominant forms of Chan/Zen practice that shaped East Asian intellectual and cultural life from the Song Dynasty through the modern period. The patronage of Linji temples by imperial courts (particularly the Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasties in China, and the Kamakura shogunate in Japan) connected the school's institutions to the highest levels of political power. Huguo (protecting the nation) temple names reflect this imperial patronage tradition.
